interactive.title: Gradient from two points
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a squared grid. Two points, A and B, sit on the grid with a straight line through them, and either can be dragged. They snap to whole-number points so the sums stay easy. Between them is a step triangle. Its run is an arrow straight across from A to the corner below or above B, labelled with its signed size, x₂ − x₁. Its rise is an arrow straight up or down from that corner to B, labelled y₂ − y₁. An arrow pointing right or up is positive and one pointing left or down is negative, because those are the ways the numbers grow and shrink on each axis. Above the grid a readout fills in m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁) with the two points' coordinates in brackets, then the rise ÷ the run, then m. When the rise and the run have the same sign m is positive, and when their signs differ m is negative. On one screen both points slide along their line, so the triangle grows and shrinks while m stays put, and the slide ends on a small step with a run of 1, whose rise is m. Dragging B level with A makes the rise 0, so m is 0. Standing B straight above A makes the run 0, and the readout says it cannot divide by 0, so the gradient is undefined. Two screens give the axes units, amps across and volts up, or minutes across and litres up, and there the rise and run are read off the scales in those units. A faint ring marks a point you can drag. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows two points and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the triangle and fills in the readout for those two points.
interactive.ignores: The points snap to whole numbers, but a line's points need not be whole numbers, and the rule is the same. The grid shows a short piece of a line that carries on both ways. On the two units screens a square across and a square up stand for different amounts, so how steep the line looks depends on the scales, and m is read from the scale values, not by counting squares: on the volts screen the triangle is 3 squares by 3, which would wrongly give 1. The readings and the tank's figures are example values, chosen to sit exactly on a line.

explain.text:
A straight line's [[gradient]], m, is how much y changes for each 1 you go along. It is the change in y ÷ change in x you met as a rate, under its usual name. To find it from two points on the line, divide the difference in their y-coordinates by the difference in their x-coordinates.[^1] Picture a step triangle between the two points. Its [[run]] is the arrow straight across, x₂ − x₁, and its [[rise]] is the arrow up or down, y₂ − y₁. For A (1, 3) and B (4, 9), the run is 4 − 1 = 3 and the rise is 9 − 3 = 6, so m = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. The line climbs 2 for each 1 along. The other way up, 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 would say it climbs half a step for each 1 along, but the triangle climbs 6 in 3 steps along, which is 2 for each. So the change in y goes on top.

Any two points on the same line give the same m. A straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along wherever you are on it, because if the climb changed from one step to the next, the line would bend. So a run of 3 is three steps of 1 with three equal climbs, and dividing the rise by 3 gives back the climb for one step. Slide A and B along the line to (2, 5) and (3, 7), and the triangle shrinks to a run of 1 and a rise of 2, which is m itself. The gradient is a measure of how steep the line is,[^2] since a bigger rise or fall for each 1 along makes a steeper line.

The arrows' directions give the sign. Going from A to B, the run is positive when B is to the right, and the rise is negative when B is lower. A negative divided by a positive is negative, so a line that falls from left to right has a negative gradient. For A (1, 7) and B (4, 1), m = (1 − 7) ÷ (4 − 1) = −6 ÷ 3 = −2. You can start from either point, as long as it comes first on top and on the bottom. Starting from B turns both arrows round, (7 − 1) ÷ (1 − 4) = 6 ÷ −3, which is still −2. Mixing the order turns only one arrow round and gives 2, the wrong sign. Put brackets round a negative coordinate, because taking away a negative adds. From (−1, −3) to (2, 3), m = (3 − (−3)) ÷ (2 − (−1)) = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. A level line has a rise of 0, and 0 divided by any run is 0, so its gradient is 0. A line straight up has a run of 0. No number times 0 gives its rise, so the rise cannot be divided by 0, and its gradient is undefined.[^3]

On a real graph the rise and run are read off the scales in the axes' units, so m is in y's unit per x's unit. For an ordinary resistor, a plot of voltage against current is approximately a straight line, and its slope is the resistance, the voltage divided by the current.[^4] Example readings of 10 V at 2 A and 25 V at 5 A give a rise of 15 V over a run of 3 A, so m = 5 V per A. Resistance is measured in volts per amp,[^5] the ohm, so that is 5 Ω. In lesson 5, a winding's resistance against its temperature plots roughly as a line, and its gradient is how many ohms the resistance changes for each 1 °C. **A line's gradient m is the difference in the y-coordinates divided by the difference in the x-coordinates of any two points on it,[^1] taken in the same order, so it is the rise for each 1 along.**

analogy.text: Say a cable costs the same for every metre. Plot the cost against the length and you get a straight line, and its gradient is the price per metre. Take any two lengths, divide the difference in cost by the difference in length, and you get that same price per metre.
analogy.breaks: The total cost only goes up as you buy more, so it never shows a falling line's negative gradient or a line straight up. If a full drum is cheaper per metre, the graph is no longer one straight line.

practice.text:
- Write the rule down first: m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
- Pick which point comes first, and keep it first on top and on the bottom.
- Put each coordinate in, in brackets.
- Work out the rise and the run from the scale values, then divide.
- When the axes have units, give m in y's unit per x's unit.
- Check the sign against a sketch.

**Rule of thumb:** y over x, rise over run. Uphill from left to right is positive, and downhill is negative.

**Worked example:** (−2, 7) and (4, −5). m = (−5 − 7) ÷ (4 − (−2)) = −12 ÷ 6 = −2. Starting from the other point gives (7 − (−5)) ÷ (−2 − 4) = 12 ÷ −6 = −2, the same. The line falls from left to right, so a negative gradient fits.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting x on top. Check which quantity is up the side, as its change goes on top.
- Losing the minus on a falling line. A sketch that falls from left to right needs a negative m.
- Dropping the brackets, so 4 − (−2) becomes 4 − 2 = 2 instead of 6.
- Mixing the order, so the top starts from one point and the bottom from the other. That flips the sign.
- Counting squares instead of reading the scales. When a square across and a square up stand for different amounts, the count gives the wrong m.
- Calling a line straight up 0. 0 belongs to a level line, whose rise is 0. A line straight up has a run of 0, so its gradient is undefined.

Points on a squared grid, a straight line through them and a step triangle between them. The volt, amp, minute and litre readings are examples.

m is the difference in y ÷ the difference in x, with the same point first in both.

checks.label: To find the gradient of a line joining two points, divide the difference in the y-coordinates by the difference in the x-coordinates: every row of working ends in its rise ÷ its run, and each puzzle accepts only that answer
Vertical lines have a gradient which is undefined: on the line straight up, and in the puzzle where B stands straight above A, the run is zero and the working ends in undefined instead of a number
The gradient is a measure of how steep the line is: with A held still, each step higher for B makes the drawn line steeper and its m bigger
The slope of the line is the resistance, or the voltage divided by the current: on the volts screen the gradient equals each reading's voltage divided by its current
The units of resistance are volts per ampere: the volts screen gives its gradient in V per A, then in ohms

Every worked number is right, row by row: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 (3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 the wrong way up), 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 2 ÷ 1 and 10 ÷ 5 = 2, 4 ÷ 2 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2 (3 × 2 = 6), −6 ÷ 3 = −2 twice, 6 ÷ 3 and −6 ÷ −3 = 2, 9 ÷ 3 = 3, 0 ÷ 4 = 0, 5 ÷ 0 and 7 ÷ 0 undefined, 15 V ÷ 3 A = 5 V per A, 200 litres ÷ 4 minutes = 50, −6 ÷ 6 = −1, and −12 ÷ 6 = 12 ÷ −6 = −2
Any two points on one straight line give the same m: on the slide screen, every pair of whole-number points along its line gives 2
The arrows give the sign: every run arrow points right exactly when its run is positive and every rise arrow up exactly when its rise is positive; starting from B turns both round but keeps m
Before an answer a puzzle draws no new triangle and its working reads ?; a right answer draws the triangle and fills in the working, and every wrong answer has a hint of its own
Every wrong answer offered is a real slip, worked from the puzzle's own points: the run over the rise, the rise alone, a lost minus, dropped brackets or a mixed order
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; a puzzle's triangle draws within 2.5 s
